title: Bank Rate rises to 4% and gilt yields sit above 5%
what_happened: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on an 8–1 vote, its first rise since August 2023, citing inflation of 3.5% heading to about 5% by mid-2027 on higher energy prices. The 10-year gilt yield was about 5.15% on the day.
client_effect: For a DB pension scheme, higher gilt yields lower the present value of promised pensions. Hedged schemes see assets and liabilities fall together; under-hedged schemes see funding improve. Schemes using leveraged LDI must hold enough collateral when yields jump. Cash and short-dated bonds now pay more, which raises the bar for every riskier asset.
decision_that_changes: How much interest-rate and inflation risk to hedge, how much collateral to hold against LDI, whether to lock in yields with buy-and-maintain credit, and whether improved funding brings buyout or run-on forward.
existing_investments: Long-dated bond and LDI portfolios lose market value as yields rise (matched by lower liabilities). Growth assets look less necessary for well-funded schemes. Money market and short-duration holdings earn more.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Review hedge ratios and collateral waterfalls with LDI clients; show cashflow-driven credit portfolios that lock in current yields; for OCIO clients, revisit the journey plan and endgame timing.
sales_angle: A prospect whose funding has just improved may reopen manager or OCIO selection. The useful opening is a specific observation about their hedge ratio or endgame date, not a product.
rm_angle: Existing clients need a clear account of what the move did to their own assets, liabilities and collateral, before they ask.
risks_counterarguments: The Bank said the move should not be read as the start of a long run of rises, yet also that it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. Yields could fall back, reversing funding gains for unhedged schemes. A rate rise driven by an energy shock can hurt growth assets and sponsor covenants at the same time.
client_question: If gilt yields moved another 100 basis points in either direction, what would happen to your funding level and your collateral position, and who would have to act?
watch: MPC decision on 17 December 2026; CPI prints; 10- and 30-year gilt yields; PPF 7800 monthly funding ratio.

title: DB schemes are in aggregate surplus and the buy-in market is busy but smaller in value
what_happened: The PPF 7800 index showed an aggregate surplus of £275.4bn and a 133.7% funding ratio at end October 2026. In 2025 a record 370 buy-ins completed, but premium fell to about £38bn from £47.8bn in 2024 as fewer multi-billion deals transacted.
client_effect: Most trustees are no longer asking how to close a deficit. They are choosing an endgame: sell the liabilities to an insurer (buy-in then buyout), or keep running the scheme ('run-on') and decide what to do with surplus.
decision_that_changes: Whether and when to approach insurers; how to reshape assets so an insurer will accept them; if running on, how to invest for cashflow and how surplus is shared.
existing_investments: Illiquid holdings become a problem for schemes heading to buyout because insurers prefer gilts, cash and investment-grade credit. Schemes that run on can keep or add contractual-income assets.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) For buyout-bound clients: portfolio transition and 'insurer-ready' credit. For run-on clients: cashflow-driven investing and OCIO. For the insurers receiving the assets: insurance asset management.
sales_angle: Winning a mandate from a scheme that plans to buy out in three years means competing for assets that will leave. The time horizon has to be part of the proposal.
rm_angle: An RM may have to help a client leave well: preparing assets for transfer to an insurer is good service that shrinks the manager's own assets.
risks_counterarguments: The s179 measure is less demanding than buyout cost, so surplus on this basis does not mean every scheme can afford an insurer. Isio found fiduciary mandate numbers fell for the first time since 2008 as schemes exited through insurance.
client_question: Is your target buyout, run-on or still open, and which of your current holdings would be hardest to hand to an insurer?
watch: Half-year bulk annuity volumes from LCP, Hymans Robertson and Aon; insurer pricing; PPF 7800.

title: Pension Schemes Act 2026: DB surplus release and superfunds
what_happened: The Act received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It lets trustees of private-sector DB schemes change rules to pay surplus to sponsors more easily (consultation 2026, regulations expected in force 2027), creates a statutory regime for DB superfunds, and provides a statutory remedy for the Virgin Media rulings.
client_effect: Running a well-funded scheme on becomes more attractive to sponsors, because surplus need not be trapped until wind-up. Trustees keep their fiduciary duties and must decide what protection members need before agreeing any release.
decision_that_changes: The buyout-versus-run-on choice, the level of funding at which surplus may be released, and the investment strategy that supports regular surplus payments.
existing_investments: A run-on scheme needs assets that generate dependable income over decades rather than a portfolio being tidied up for an insurer.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Offer run-on modelling, cashflow-driven portfolios and OCIO governance for sponsors who decide to keep schemes. This is a provider's commercial interest and trustees should test it against insurer pricing.
sales_angle: Run-on lengthens the life of the asset pool an asset manager can serve, which is why managers favour it. A credible salesperson says so and still shows the buyout comparison.
rm_angle: Explain what is law now and what waits for 2027 regulations, so trustees do not act on headlines.
risks_counterarguments: Detailed rules were not in force at the cutoff. Member representatives may resist releases. A future fall in yields or a credit event could remove the surplus after it has been paid out.
client_question: What would have to be true about funding, covenant and member protection before your trustees would agree to release any surplus?
watch: DWP consultation and draft regulations on surplus; TPR guidance; first publicised surplus releases.

title: Pension Schemes Act 2026 and Mansion House Accord: DC scale and private markets
what_happened: The Act requires master trust and group personal pension default arrangements to reach £25bn by 2030 (or be on track by 2035), with the requirement starting no earlier than 1 January 2030, and creates a reserve power, usable 2028–2032, to require minimum private-market and UK allocations. Separately, 17 providers signed the voluntary Mansion House Accord in May 2025 to hold 10% of default funds in private markets by 2030, half of it in the UK.
client_effect: DC providers below scale must merge or grow. The surviving providers are few and large, run tight fee budgets, and need private-market exposure in a form that fits daily-dealt default funds.
decision_that_changes: Which providers survive; how defaults obtain private-market exposure (for example Long-Term Asset Funds); which external managers are kept as the number of buyers shrinks.
existing_investments: Low-cost index building blocks remain the core. Small specialist allocations are at risk when defaults are merged.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Offer private-market and multi-asset components designed for DC defaults. GS's actual position in UK DC was not established in this research.
sales_angle: Fewer, bigger buyers mean long sales cycles with investment teams and consultants, and severe price pressure.
rm_angle: A manager inside a default that is being consolidated has to re-earn its place with the acquiring provider.
risks_counterarguments: The Accord is voluntary and conditional on suitable assets. The reserve power had not been used. Higher-cost private assets must show value under the value-for-money framework. Scale targets may be met by a handful of incumbents, leaving little room for new managers.
client_question: How will you reach your private-market target inside your charge budget, and what would make you remove a manager from the default?
watch: DWP regulations on scale and value for money; master trust mergers; LTAF launches; Accord progress reports.

title: LGPS 'Fit for the Future': six pools and delegated implementation
what_happened: Local Government Pension Scheme pools fell from eight to six after Brunel's and ACCESS's proposals were not accepted, with funds joining other pools from 1 April 2026. Regulations in force from 30 June 2026 require each fund to delegate implementation of its investment strategy to its pool and to take its principal investment advice from the pool. Pool companies must hold full regulatory authorisation by 30 September 2027.
client_effect: The council pension fund still sets strategy, but the pool company chooses and manages investments. Pools are building internal management and concentrating external mandates.
decision_that_changes: Who an asset manager must convince: the pool's investment team rather than 80-plus individual committees and their consultants.
existing_investments: Legacy mandates held directly by funds must move into pool vehicles; some will be merged or ended during transition.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Cover the six pools as a small number of large, sophisticated accounts; offer strategies pools cannot easily run internally.
sales_angle: A handful of very large tenders replaces many small ones. Losing one is costly and the next chance may be years away.
rm_angle: During transition the task is to protect service quality while assets are restructured, and to accept that some mandates will end for reasons unrelated to performance.
risks_counterarguments: Full asset transfer is running behind the original March 2026 target. Internal management by pools reduces the external-manager opportunity. Whether GS holds LGPS mandates was not established.
client_question: Which capabilities do you intend to build in-house over the next three years, and where will you still want an external partner?
watch: Pool onboarding progress; 31 March 2027 investment strategy statements; 30 September 2027 authorisation deadline; pool tenders.

title: OCIO moves up-market while the UK fiduciary market total stays flat
what_happened: GSAM won the roughly £23bn BAE Systems mandate in 2023 (with the in-house team transferring) and a roughly $40bn multi-country Shell mandate in 2025, and reported $480bn of global OCIO assets under supervision at 31 March 2026. Isio's 2025 survey found UK fiduciary assets flat at £241bn and mandate numbers down 4%, with partial 'OCIO' mandates now 53% of assets.
client_effect: Large sponsors are asking whether running an in-house pension investment team is core business, especially as schemes mature and need hedging and cashflow skills more than growth investing.
decision_that_changes: Keep an in-house team, outsource implementation while keeping strategy, or delegate fully. Each changes who is accountable, what it costs and how easily the decision can be reversed.
existing_investments: On appointment the OCIO takes over manager selection and implementation; existing managers may be replaced, including by the OCIO's own funds.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Compete for the small number of very large schemes, offering scale, private-market access and, where relevant, continuity for the in-house team.
sales_angle: These are multi-year pursuits run through a regulated tender with a third-party evaluator. A few decisions move tens of billions.
rm_angle: The provider becomes responsible for outcomes it used to only advise on, under scrutiny from an independent oversight adviser and with fees benchmarked at each review.
risks_counterarguments: The pool of schemes shrinks as they buy out. Concentration risk in a few large clients. Conflict-of-interest scrutiny when an OCIO allocates to in-house products. Other providers also win awards and mandates (Shell's Dutch fund chose BlackRock; the 2026 UK Pensions Awards fiduciary category went to Van Lanschot Kempen).
client_question: Which decisions do you want to keep, which do you want to delegate, and how would you get them back if you changed your mind?
watch: Isio's next fiduciary management survey; further large in-house teams outsourcing; mandate re-tenders.

title: Fiduciary manager tendering rules shape every OCIO sale
what_happened: Since 1 October 2022 pensions regulations overseen by The Pensions Regulator (replacing the Competition and Markets Authority's 2019 Order) require trustees to run a competitive tender, inviting at least three unconnected providers, before fiduciary managers run 20% or more of scheme assets. Trustees must also set objectives for investment consultants.
client_effect: Trustees cannot simply hand a mandate to their existing consultant's fiduciary arm. They normally hire a third-party evaluator to run the selection.
decision_that_changes: The selection process: longlist, request for proposal, scorecard, site visits, and comparison of fees and performance on a common standard.
existing_investments: Appointments made before the rules without a qualifying tender had to be re-tendered.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Maintain relationships with evaluators and consultants, and respond to formal requests for proposal with standardised performance data.
sales_angle: The evaluator is a gatekeeper. Much of the work is written: questionnaires, fee templates, track records.
rm_angle: Incumbents are re-tested at reviews; documented objectives make underperformance visible.
risks_counterarguments: Tendering raises cost and favours providers with resources to bid. The rule is old news; its value in interview is explaining why the process looks the way it does.
client_question: Who is advising you on the selection, and what did your scorecard weight most heavily last time?
watch: TPR guidance updates; evaluator market share.

title: Investment consultants are consolidating into larger groups
what_happened: Several UK pensions consultancies changed hands in 2024–2026: Mercer completed its purchase of Cardano; Howden bought Barnett Waddingham; Gallagher bought Redington; Howden agreed to buy Hymans Robertson's insurance consulting team.
client_effect: Trustees have fewer independent advisers to choose from, and more of them belong to groups that also sell fiduciary management or insurance broking.
decision_that_changes: Which adviser trustees regard as independent enough to oversee an OCIO or run a tender.
existing_investments: No direct effect; adviser changes can trigger strategy and manager reviews.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B) Consultant-relations coverage must track which research teams and buy-lists survive each merger.
sales_angle: A manager's rating with a merged consultant research team can decide access to many schemes at once.
rm_angle: When a client's adviser is acquired, expect a review of every manager.
risks_counterarguments: Only the Mercer–Cardano completion was confirmed on a fetched page; other details come from search-result summaries and need checking before being quoted.
client_question: Has your adviser's change of ownership altered how you think about conflicts between advice and fiduciary management?
watch: Further deals; regulatory attention to adviser conflicts.
